well the time for the class is almost here!

I got a few holograms for the gallery display from the members of the forum, a nice one from Kris Meerlo, and one from Adam, and dave is sending one. anyone who wants to display their hologram at the gallery at the last day of the class PM me.

I have done lots of reading and testing in the process of 1800's when photography began. one I took glossy laser printing paper and soaked in silver nitrate and then washed in tap water which has chloride in it (which makes silver chloride) then contact copied with a old 4x5 neg then developed and fixed... wow it looks nice.

what really got my attenting was the Collodion process which led to b/w film as we know it today. what was so intresting was how they made the plates, they mixed the (iodide/bromide) to the collodion then coated the plates.

then to finish the process of making the plates put it in a bath of silver nitrate.

now there has been test in holography plate making where the silver nitrate was mixed with the gel and then coated to the plate, and then after they have dried put them in a bromide bath... but what if it was done in the same order as they did in the collodion process? this would be very intresting to try for making hologram plates

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> now there has been test in holography plate making where the silver nitrate was mixed with the gel and then coated to the plate, and then after they have dried put them in a bromide bath... but what if it was done in the same order as they did in the collodion process? this would be very intresting to try for making hologram plates

Yes, that might work Danny. But the problem you would get there is that the bath of AgNO3 would likely be ruined after one dip of a plate into it. And since the AgNO3 spoils quickly and the LiBr is cheaper, it's more cost efficient to first load the plate with AgNO3 and then dip into a LiBr solution.
